title: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting (part 1 of 3)
sources: Positions: authored, replayed with python-chess, engine-checked by tools/validate_lessons.py

steps.text: Picture a game where you leave a piece on a square and a pawn you never noticed takes it for free. Most lost pieces go this way: one attacker or defender was left uncounted. This lesson gives you a short habit that catches it.

steps.caption: Two white units attack the knight; one black pawn defends it. Two attackers against one defender.

steps.text: Every capture fight happens on one square. Count the **attackers**: the pieces that could capture there. Then count the **defenders**: the other side's pieces that could take back. Do both counts before you move anything. In the position above it is 2 against 1. The numbers alone do not give the answer, but without them you are guessing.
A **loose** piece is attacked and has no defender, so it can be taken for free. Count it as 1 against 0.

steps.title: Same count, different target and first capturer
steps.prompt: Again two attackers and one defender. This time the target is a pawn and the first attacker is a knight. Predict first: does the count still win?

steps.caption: One attacker, no defenders. This is the loose piece from earlier, seen as a count: 1 against 0.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. Nothing can take back, so White wins 3 points.
Black cannot win the knight back. White is a knight ahead.

steps.caption: Count for your own piece too. Before the rook steps to d5, ask who attacks that square: the pawn on e6 does, and nothing of White's defends it.

line.say: The rook lands where a pawn attacks it and nothing defends it.
The pawn takes it for free. One look at the count would have stopped this.

steps.caption: Again 1 attacker, but now 1 defender, and the attacker is worth more than the target.

line.say: The defending pawn takes the rook: -5. White gave 5 points for 1.

steps.text: A fight on one square is a string of swaps: capture, take back, capture again. Each side may stop when the next capture would cost more than it wins. Add the points as you go, using the counting values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. Those values are a rule of thumb [I], not the true worth of a piece.

steps.caption: Back to the opening position. The pawn goes first: the cheapest attacker.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight: +3, and the cheapest White piece did it.
Black's pawn takes back: -1. White's running total is +2.
The knight takes the last pawn: +1. Total +3, and Black has no defender left.

steps.text: The first piece to capture is the one the defender takes. If it is worth more than what it captured, you start behind and need the last capture to win it back. So send your cheapest attacker first. [I] That is a rule of thumb; a pin or a hidden piece can change who is able to recapture.

steps.caption: The pawn on d5 is attacked by a pawn and a rook, and defended once. Start with the pawn.

line.say: The rook takes the last pawn: +1. Nothing can take the rook, so White wins a pawn.

steps.caption: The same position, but the rook goes first. Same pieces, same squares, a different result.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn: +1, but now a rook stands where a pawn can take it.
Black's pawn takes the rook: -5. Running total -4.
White's pawn takes back: +1. Total -3. Two pawns won, a rook lost.

steps.text: Edward Lasker, in *Chess Strategy*, advised totalling what each side can capture with before starting, not playing the line out in your head. The boards here play it out so you can see each step; totals are the method to aim for. Znosko-Borovsky, in *The Middle Game in Chess*, counted attackers needed against defenders available around a king; the same habit of counting both sides first carries over to one square.

**Remember.** Before a capture fight on one square, count the attackers and the defenders. A piece that is attacked and has no defender is loose and can be taken for free. Add up the points swap by swap, and send your cheapest attacker first. The values are a rule of thumb, and a pin can change who can recapture.
